items.title: 18.7.1 Ligand Exchange Reactions of Copper(II) Complexes

source_refs.note: Topic 18.7.1 (PDF 28); Figures 18.7 and 18.8 are replaced by an original diagram, and the precipitate-dissolving equation is taken from Quick Check 18.5.

blocks.text: Cu2+(aq) actually means the complex ion [Cu(H2O)6]2+, which gives copper(II) salt solutions, such as copper sulphate solution, their blue colour.

blocks.caption: Ligand exchange reactions of copper(II)
rows: blue solution gives a light blue precipitate; two OH- replace two H2O
excess conc. NH3 on the precipitate
precipitate dissolves to a dark blue solution
blue to dark blue; four NH3 replace four H2O

blocks.alt: Three test tubes: blue [Cu(H2O)6]2+ in the middle ('start here'); conc. HCl turns it into yellow-green [CuCl4]2- (tetrahedral), conc. NH3 into dark blue [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (octahedral). Below, NaOH gives a light blue precipitate of [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2], and the octahedral ammine ion is drawn with four NH3 in a plane and two H2O above and below.
blocks.caption: Ligand exchange and colour changes of copper(II) complexes (original diagram after Figures 18.7 and 18.8).
blocks.long_description: Starting from the blue hexaaquacopper(II) ion, different ligands give different colours. Two hydroxide ions replace two water molecules to give a light blue precipitate, which dissolves in excess ammonia. Ammonia replaces four water molecules to give the dark blue [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+, an octahedral ion with the four NH3 in a square and the two H2O on the axis. Concentrated hydrochloric acid replaces all six waters with four chloride ions, giving yellow-green tetrahedral [CuCl4]2-; adding water reverses this.
